title: Saudi OpenAI Employee's Arrest Revives Fears US Tech Companies Are Hiring Spies - Slashdot

content_html:
That Saudi national working at OpenAI and arrested by the FBI "has not been charged with foreign espionage," writes the Washington Post, "and the U.S. government has not said whether he was acting alone or as an agent of a foreign government."

But "there are signs that the U.S. government is exploring the latter possibility," they add, citing comments from Chris McGuire, a member of the National Security Council during the Biden administration: The Department of Justice's press release about the incident says that the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control section, whose responsibility includes prosecuting spies, is assisting with the case... A Washington-based Middle East expert, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid incurring wrath from Saudi Arabia, said he believed the Saudi government was almost certainly involved in some way. "No one does this, not even for patriotism, without getting paid," said the person. And money would not be distributed without agreement by the Saudi royal court, he said. The Saudis lag behind their regional rival, the United Arab Emirates, in artificial intelligence development, he added.
Friday America's Director of National Intelligence told CNBC that espionage, "both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities. It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of." (And CNBC adds that"An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is 'probably the tip of the iceberg.'")

The suspect had recently said he helped advise government agencies in Saudi Arabia on technology, reports the New York Times: In an Arabic podcast interview last month, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, said he and other Saudi tech professionals in Silicon Valley had formed a group that advised Saudi organizations, including the kingdom's social insurance agency...

"Silicon Valley is ground zero for espionage from a variety of countries around the world," said Amy Zegart, a professor at Stanford University who specializes in national security and intelligence. She added that she was "troubled" by the OpenAI incident and expected more cases "because these companies are so important."


The Washington Post says the arrest "has ignited a fierce debate about the potential risks of Silicon Valley's international workforce — employees who often hail from nations seeking to rival the AI superpower status of the U.S." Foreign nationals have long formed the backbone of the American tech industry, helping U.S. companies surpass their would-be international rivals... As recently as April, Katrina Mulligan, a senior member of OpenAI's national security team, called for an "accelerated pathway to citizenship" for such workers, referring to foreign hires as a "national strategic asset" at an event on Capitol Hill. She estimated that a significant number of OpenAI's employees were not U.S. citizens, including Chinese nationals. Just half of the 300 top AI researchers in the world, she said, were American.

Other industry leaders — as well as some lawmakers — have long accused top-tier tech companies with many foreign workers of disadvantaging Americans and being breeding grounds for Chinese espionage. Palmer Luckey, CEO of weapons maker Anduril, and venture capitalist Shaun Maguire of Sequoia Capital took to X on Wednesday to revisit arguments that the industry should focus on hiring U.S. citizens. "Silicon Valley has operated with maximum openness and maximum naivete toward foreign tradecraft," Maguire wrote... At OpenAI on Wednesday, employees continued tense conversations about the political implications of the arrest for immigrant workers, two OpenAI employees said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions... The arrest triggered a discussion on OpenAI's internal Slack messaging platform among employees about whether the incident might increase pressure from the Trump administration on OpenAI to not hire foreign nationals, said one of the people.

In March, Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, wrote in court papers that AI developer Anthropic's reliance on staff with ties to China was among the concerns that fueled the Defense Department's conflict with the AI company.

《华盛顿邮报》写道，这名在 OpenAI 工作并被联邦调查局逮捕的沙特国民“并未被指控从事外国间谍活动”，“美国政府也没有透露他是单独行动还是作为外国政府特工行事”。

但“有迹象表明，美国政府正在探索后一种可能性，”他们补充道，并引用了拜登政府期间国家安全委员会成员克里斯·麦奎尔的评论：司法部关于该事件的新闻稿称，负责起诉间谍的国家安全部反情报和出口管制部门正在协助此案…… 一位驻华盛顿的中东专家表示，他相信沙特政府几乎肯定以某种方式参与其中。为避免激怒沙特阿拉伯，该专家要求匿名。 这位人士表示：“没有人会在没有报酬的情况下这样做，即使是出于爱国主义。” 他说，未经沙特王室同意，不会分配资金。 他补充说，沙特在人工智能开发方面落后于其地区竞争对手阿拉伯联合酋长国。 周五，美国国家情报总监告诉 CNBC，间谍活动“无论是商业间谍活动，还是国家支持的间谍活动，都是现实。 这是我们的私营企业需要警惕的事情。” （CNBC 补充道，“一位因讨论非公开信息而要求不透露姓名的前中央情报局官员本周告诉 CNBC，此案‘可能只是冰山一角。’”）

据《纽约时报》报道，嫌疑人最近表示，他帮助为沙特阿拉伯政府机构提供技术方面的建议：35 岁的沙特公民阿卜杜拉赫曼·阿尔福赞 (Abdulrahman Alfozan) 上个月在接受阿拉伯语播客采访时表示，他和硅谷的其他沙特技术专业人士组成了一个小组，为包括沙特社会保险机构在内的沙特组织提供建议…… 斯坦福大学专门研究国家安全和情报的教授艾米·泽加特说：“硅谷是来自世界各地的间谍活动的归零地。” 她补充说，她对 OpenAI 事件感到“困扰”，并预计会出现更多案例，“因为这些公司非常重要”。 《华盛顿邮报》称，这次逮捕“引发了一场关于硅谷国际劳动力潜在风险的激烈争论——这些员工往往来自寻求与美国人工智能超级大国地位相抗衡的国家”。外国人长期以来一直是美国科技行业的支柱，帮助美国公司超越潜在的国际竞争对手...... 就在今年 4 月，OpenAI 国家安全团队的高级成员卡特里娜·穆里根 (Katrina Mulligan) 呼吁为此类工人“加速获得公民身份的途径”，并在国会山的一次活动中将外国雇员称为“国家战略资产”。 她估计 OpenAI 的大量员工不是美国公民，其中包括中国公民。 她说，世界上 300 名顶尖人工智能研究人员中只有一半是美国人。 其他行业领袖以及一些立法者长期以来一直指责拥有许多外国工人的顶级科技公司对美国人不利，并成为中国间谍活动的滋生地。 武器制造商 Anduril 首席执行官 Palmer Luckey 和红杉资本风险投资家 Shaun Maguire 周三在 X 上重新审视了该行业应专注于雇用美国公民的论点。 马奎尔写道：“硅谷对外国贸易技术采取了最大程度的开放性和最大程度的天真态度。” 两名 OpenAI 员工表示，周三在 OpenAI 上，员工们继续就逮捕移民工人的政治影响进行紧张的对话，他们要求匿名描述内部讨论情况…… 一位知情人士表示，这次逮捕引发了员工在 OpenAI 内部 Slack 消息平台上的讨论，讨论这一事件是否会增加特朗普政府对 OpenAI 的压力，要求其不要雇用外国人。 今年 3 月，五角大楼首席技术官埃米尔·迈克尔 (Emil Michael) 在法庭文件中写道，人工智能开发商 Anthropic 对与中国有联系的员工的依赖是加剧国防部与人工智能公司冲突的担忧之一。
